title: Hidden-line removal
text:
Hidden-line algorithms published before 1984[1,2,3,4] divide edges into line segments by the intersection points of their images, and then test each segment for visibility against each face of the model. Assuming a model of a collection of polyhedra with the boundary of each topologically equivalent to a sphere and with faces topologically equivalent to disks, according to Euler's formula, there are Θ(n) faces. Testing Θ(n2) line segments against Θ(n) faces takes Θ(n3) time in the worst case.[5] Appel's algorithm[1] is also unstable, because an error in visibility will be propagated to subsequent segment endpoints.[6]

Ottmann and Widmayer[7]

and Ottmann, Widmayer and Wood[8]

proposed O((n + k) log2 n)-time hidden-line algorithms. Then Nurmi improved[9] the running time to O((n + k) log n). In the worst case, these algorithms take Θ(n2 log2 n) and Θ(n2 log n) time respectively, but they can be faster in practice if k is less than quadratic.

Any hidden-line algorithm has to determine the union of Θ(n) hidden intervals on n edges in the worst case. As Ω(n log n) is a lower bound for determining the union of n intervals,[10]

it appears that the best one can hope to achieve is Θ(n2 log n) worst-case time, and hence Nurmi's algorithm is optimal.

However, the log n factor was eliminated by Devai,[5] who raised the open problem whether the same optimal O(n2) upper bound existed for hidden-surface removal. This problem was solved by McKenna in 1987.[11]

The intersection-sensitive algorithms[7,8,9] are mainly known in the computational-geometry literature. The quadratic upper bounds are also appreciated by the computer-graphics literature: Ghali notes[12] that the algorithms by Devai and McKenna "represent milestones in visibility algorithms", breaking a theoretical barrier from O(n2 log n) to O(n2) for processing a scene of n edges.

The other open problem, raised by Devai,[5] of whether there exists an O(n log n + v)-time hidden-line algorithm, where v, as noted above, is the number of visible segments, is still unsolved at the time of writing.
